sm: The author argues that believing Christians should spend the next two years laboring for one scenario and preparing for another. The first is reformation and revival, through preaching, planting churches, prayer, building schools, having children and starting businesses, which he calls a Black Swan Revival. The second is principled resistance to genuine tyranny, which requires a better theological understanding of Romans thirteen, a lesson he says the COVID period exposed. He explains his title, Sweet Defiance, as the idea that resisting tyranny is obedience to God and therefore sweet. He then says Democratic socialists want to abolish the Senate and Electoral College and subordinate the presidency and Supreme Court to an expanded House, and that states should declare ahead of 2028 that they will refuse to comply, like sanctuary states. He begins a thought experiment about a socialist nominee promising to be president for life.

Continuing the thought experiment, the author imagines that nominee winning on promises of free everything, and Donald Trump then announcing that he will be president for life instead. He says the Constitution would be wrecked, but the blame would fall on the electorate and on ministers who refused to preach the whole counsel of God, citing John Adams on a Constitution made for a moral and religious people. If the socialists have a good night in 2028, states should answer with a cheerful unwillingness to comply and keep their republican form of government. For preparation, he recommends reading Protestant resistance works, including Glenn Sunshine's book on slaying Leviathan and a sixteenth century Huguenot work. He also urges learning real definitions, such as fascism as a state-controlled economy, which he says the left projects onto others. He advises working with other conservatives while avoiding malice and stupidity in leaders, and begins his seven principles with worshiping God wholeheartedly.

The author continues his seven principles. It is never right to obey man rather than God, resisting those who subvert lawful authority is not resisting lawful authority, and abusers of authority must not decide what counts as abuse. Protestant resistance is layered, moving from verbal testimony, to fleeing, to defensive armed action meant to thwart rather than overthrow, and lesser magistrates such as governors and county commissioners are ideally placed to say no. He compares tyrannical measures to the ignored Metric Conversion Act of 1975. He then names three groups of voices to tune out. These are Republican squishes, hotheads he likens to Boromir who think it is time to act, and pietists, from whom he expects the most trouble because they refuse to learn about politics and favor an imaginary high road.
